faqs.q: Something is digging up my McCormick lawn at night and it smells like skunk. What is going on?
faqs.a: That combination is a striped skunk hunting grubs — the small cone-shaped holes across a lawn are its signature — and a den under a porch, deck, or crawlspace edge is usually nearby. Skunks are South Carolina's number-two rabies carrier in Department of Public Health testing, and routine relocation is against state law, so our crew traps calmly at the den with covered traps, handles the animal under SCDNR depredation rules, and screens the den opening so the next skunk finds it closed.

faqs.q: Are armadillos really established around McCormick?
faqs.a: Yes. Nine-banded armadillos are established throughout the entirety of South Carolina, and around here they burrow under porches, driveways, and crawlspace edges and root up lawns hunting grubs and worms. We trap the animals working your property and backfill and screen the burrow openings, because an open burrow in this soil is quickly claimed by the next armadillo — or by a skunk or opossum.

faqs.q: I saw a snake near my Parksville home. Should I be worried?
faqs.a: Most snakes our crew is called about here are harmless rat snakes, black racers, and garter snakes following rodents and frogs. The ones that change the call are the copperhead, which is statewide, and — only in the wet coastal and swamp country — the cottonmouth. We identify first, from a safe distance: keep kids and pets inside, do not try to move or kill it, and tell us where it went. The southern hognose snake of the Sandhills is State Threatened and is never handled as a removal job, and venomous snakes are safety-and-referral work, not a guaranteed capture.

faqs.q: I found a raccoon in my Plum Branch attic — can you move it to the woods?
faqs.a: We do not promise that, because South Carolina does not allow it: SCDNR states that routine relocation of wildlife is against state law, and a captured animal must be destroyed or, with a separate department permit, may be relocated. What our crew does is eviction and exclusion — the raccoon leaves through a one-way door or is removed under SCDNR depredation rules, and then we seal every entry in steel so the attic stays closed. Raccoons are also South Carolina's leading rabies carrier in the Department of Public Health's testing, so attic latrines get cleaned and sanitized, not just emptied.

faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a Plum Branch home?
faqs.a: Bat work here is exclusion only, and no permit is required to remove bats in South Carolina. What controls the timing is SCDNR guidance, which we follow: complete exclusions are planned for early spring (March-April) or fall (August-October), and we do not run a full exclusion from May through mid-July, sometimes into August, because flightless pups would be trapped inside. That window is agency guidance, not a state law. We can inspect and map every entry at any time of year, and a bat found inside your living space is different — keep the room closed and call us, because bats in living quarters are a rabies-testing situation handled with the Department of Public Health.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Plum Branch?
faqs.a: It depends on the parcel more than the species — a raccoon in one chimney is a small job; a farmstead with animals across the house and barn, plus a beaver reach in the branch, is a programme. We survey the whole property first and quote the complete job firmly before work begins, so distance does not turn into per-trip billing surprises. Removal runs under a depredation permit for your property, and for beaver that permit runs a full year, which suits how lake-country water actually has to be managed.

faqs.q: Armadillos are digging up our Plum Branch yard and under the porch. What does removal involve?
faqs.a: Trapping the animals working your ground, then closing what they dug. Armadillos hold a home range and return to proven burrows; in McCormick County's soils an emptied burrow under a porch or at a slab edge gets re-let quickly, so backfilling and screening the openings is part of the same job. We will also tell you honestly if grub pressure in the lawn is feeding the rooting — trapping plus closing the burrows, with the food source named, is the combination that ends it rather than pausing it.

Plum Branch is a crossroads in McCormick County's lake country — a small community in the pine and hardwood country west of Strom Thurmond Lake, where the roads run through forest and farm and the houses stand far apart. Its wildlife work is the deep-rural version: raccoons in the farmhouse chimneys and the attics of the older homes, bats in the tall roof voids, groundhogs in the field banks and road cuts, skunks under the porches, and beaver work in the creeks feeding the Savannah River system. Around Plum Branch, the woods are not at the edge of the property; the property is a clearing in the woods.

The lake shapes the second half of the log. Thurmond Lake's wooded shoreline and the creeks running to it hold a standing population that commutes through the community's rural roads — properties near the water or on the creek branches get the pressure first and worst. Our Plum Branch inspections survey the whole parcel, house and outbuildings together, because at this density of cover a partial job is just a relocation within the same fence line.
Plum Branch.extendedBody:
Lake country, creek bottoms, and the farmstead read

Plum Branch's ground work follows its water: beavers in the branches, backing water over the low fields and farm drives; groundhogs holding the sunny banks; armadillos — established across South Carolina, this county included — rooting the yards and digging at the slabs. Beaver removal runs on the state's one-year depredation permit for the species (§50-11-2570(A)), the lawful basis for a season of management on a reach rather than a single visit. Overhead, the older homes' attics hold big brown bat colonies, excluded by SCDNR's guidance: never sealed while pups are flightless, excluded completely when the timing is right.

South Carolina's rules, plainly

There is no SCDNR operator license — the agency keeps a referral list, and that is all. Our Plum Branch work runs on depredation permits issued for your property, naming the species; the permits are free and are the legal instrument for removal in this state. Rabies-suspect animals are a public-health matter handled through SC DPH. An operator who cannot explain that framework is telling you something about the rest of the job.

Distance and the one-pass survey

McCormick County properties are far apart and farther from town, so we plan Plum Branch work as complete surveys: every structure ranked, removal and sealing sequenced in one programme. The returns, when the work needs them, are for trapping runs and seasonal timing — not for discovering the barn on the second trip.

We walk the whole fence line and barn perimeter with you. Owners usually know the two obvious systems; the survey finds the third, which is typically the one in the horses' or cattle's path.

Mount Carmel is one of McCormick County's old communities — a small settlement with a long memory, standing in the rolling forest-and-farm country between the county's lake shore and its interior. Its wildlife work matches its scale: unhurried, rural, and whole-property. Raccoons in the chimneys and barn lofts of the older homes, bats in the tall attics, groundhogs in the pasture banks, skunks under the porches, and the creek branches carrying beaver problems to the low farms. Nothing in Mount Carmel is far from the woods, and the woods keep their own schedule.

The community's older housing carries the standard rural entry list — open eaves, unscreened crawlspaces, brick chimneys without caps — and its properties share the farmstead pattern: a raccoon's territory here typically includes the house, a barn, and a well house, used in rotation. Our Mount Carmel inspections are parcel surveys by default, because single-building work in country like this is how annual wildlife subscriptions get started.
Mount Carmel.extendedBody:
Whole-parcel work in the interior

Mount Carmel sits away from the lake crowds, in the county's farm-and-forest interior, and its calls are the interior's: groundhogs in the banks and under the outbuildings, raccoons across the farmstead's roofs, snakes in the woodpiles and barn corners, and creek beavers in the wet years. The work is sequenced across the parcel — residents removed under depredation permits, structures sealed in an order that leaves no building to rotate into, burrow entrances in the worked ground collapsed or screened. Beaver permits run a year under §50-11-2570(A); most other species run thirty days, and we plan the programme to the permit, not the other way round.

The credential question, answered straight

South Carolina does not license wildlife control operators. SCDNR maintains a referral list; it is not a license, an endorsement, or an inspection regime. The legal instrument for removal is the depredation permit for your property, and the handling rules attached to it — bats excluded by SCDNR guidance on timing rather than sealed with flightless pups inside, rabies-suspect animals reported through SC DPH — are the substance behind the paperwork. Ask any operator to explain that framework; the explanation is the credential.

Attics in the old homes

Mount Carmel's pre-war homes hold the county's quietest colonies: big brown bats in the tall roof voids, sometimes for years before the staining shows. Exclusion here is a mapping job first — every gap on a layered old roofline — then a complete seal in the right season. Done fully, an old house in the woods stays empty of everything but its owners.
